::: {.callout-note .objectives}
## Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

- explain in your own words what R is and what it is typically used for;
- describe the main parts of the R ecosystem (CRAN, the tidyverse, Quarto, Shiny);
- install R and an IDE (RStudio Desktop or Positron) on your own computer;
- recognise the four panes of RStudio and what each one is for;
- install and load a package with `install.packages()` and `library()`.
:::




::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
# This lesson uses base R only: nothing to load.
```
:::


## 1. Why learn a programming language for data?

Imagine you have a spreadsheet with measurements of 344 penguins: species, island, bill length, body mass. Your supervisor asks:

- *"What is the average body mass of each species?"*
- *"Make me a plot comparing them."*
- *"Is the difference larger than what we would expect by chance?"*
- *"Oh, and we just got new data from 2025 — can you redo everything?"*

With point-and-click software you would repeat every step by hand, and in two months nobody (including you) would remember exactly which buttons were pressed. With a programming language you write the steps down **once**, as a script. Re-running the analysis on new data is then a single click, and anyone can read the script to see exactly what was done. This property is called **reproducibility**, and it is one of the main reasons scientists and analysts use code.

R is a language designed precisely for this kind of work. Here is the penguin question answered in R — you do not need to understand the code yet, just notice how short it is:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
tapply(penguins$body_mass, penguins$species, mean, na.rm = TRUE)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>    Adelie Chinstrap    Gentoo 
#>      3701      3733      5076
```


:::
:::


By the end of this course you will be able to write code like this (and much more) on your own.

## 2. What is R?

**R** is a free, open-source programming language and software environment for **statistics, data analysis and graphics**. It was created in the early 1990s by Ross Ihaka and Robert Gentleman at the University of Auckland, and it is now developed by the *R Core Team* and a very large community of contributors.

A few features make R distinctive:

- **It was built by statisticians, for data.** Vectors, tables, missing values (`NA`) and statistical models are part of the language itself, not add-ons.
- **It is interactive.** You type a command, R answers immediately. This makes exploring data fast.
- **It is extensible through packages.** A *package* is a bundle of functions, data and documentation written by someone else that you can install with one line of code.
- **It is free.** Free as in "no licence fee", and free as in "you can read and modify the source code".

Most R packages are written in R itself; parts that need to be very fast are often written in C, C++ or Fortran and called from R. You get the speed without having to write that code yourself.

### What is R used for?

| Area | Typical tasks |
|---|---|
| Statistics | descriptive statistics, hypothesis tests, regression, mixed models, survival analysis, Bayesian models |
| Data wrangling | importing, cleaning, reshaping and joining data from files and databases |
| Visualisation | publication-quality plots, maps, interactive graphics |
| Machine learning | classification, regression, clustering, dimensionality reduction |
| Communication | reports, articles, slides, websites and dashboards that mix code, text and results |

A typical data analysis follows the cycle **import → tidy → transform → visualise → model → communicate**. R has well-developed tools for every step, and this course follows exactly that path.

## 3. R compared with other tools

There is no single "best" tool: each one is a trade-off between how quickly you can start and how far it can take you.

| Tool | Strengths | Limitations for data analysis |
|---|---|---|
| **Spreadsheets** (Excel, LibreOffice, Google Sheets) | Immediate, visual, everybody has one | Hard to reproduce, error-prone with large data, limited statistics |
| **Point-and-click statistics software** (e.g. SPSS, JASP, jamovi) | Gentle learning curve, menus for common tests | Less flexible; analyses can be harder to automate and share |
| **R** | Very wide range of statistical methods, strong graphics, reports with Quarto | A programming language: there is a learning curve at the start |
| **Python** | General-purpose language, strong in machine learning and software engineering | Statistical modelling and reporting rely on several separate libraries |
| **Commercial statistical languages** (e.g. SAS, Stata) | Mature, well documented, common in some industries | Paid licences; smaller open ecosystem |

R and Python are the two most widely used open-source languages for data science, and they **cooperate** rather than compete: you can call Python from R (with the `reticulate` package) and vice versa. The concepts you learn here — data frames, vectors, functions, models — transfer directly.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Which language should I learn first?

The honest answer: the one used by the people around you. Learning *statistical thinking* and a clean *data workflow* matters far more than the specific language. Once you master one language, picking up the second is much easier.
:::

### Is R difficult?

R has a reputation for being quirky, and some of its older functions are indeed inconsistent. Two developments made it much friendlier:

1. **The tidyverse** — a family of packages (`dplyr`, `ggplot2`, `tidyr`, `readr`, …) that share a consistent design, so that once you learn one, the others feel familiar.
2. **Modern IDEs** (see Section 5) that offer auto-completion, inline help and error highlighting.

R also scales further than most beginners expect: it can talk to databases, to big-data engines such as Spark, use several CPU cores in parallel, and run deep-learning models through interfaces to Keras and Torch.

## 4. The R ecosystem

When people say "R" they often mean the language **plus** everything around it.

| Component | What it is |
|---|---|
| **CRAN** | The *Comprehensive R Archive Network*: the official repository of R packages. It hosts more than twenty thousand packages, each checked automatically on several operating systems. |
| **Bioconductor** | A repository of packages for bioinformatics and genomics. |
| **The tidyverse** | A collection of packages for data science with a common grammar. You will use it from [Lesson 9](../02-data/09-dplyr-verbs.qmd) onwards. |
| **Quarto** | A publishing system that turns a document mixing text and code into HTML, PDF, Word, slides or a website. *This course website is built with Quarto.* |
| **Shiny** | A package for building interactive web applications directly from R, without writing HTML or JavaScript. |
| **webR** | R compiled to run inside a web browser. It powers the interactive exercises on this site. |

You can try R right now, without installing anything: the box below runs real R **in your browser**.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
```{webr}
# Press "Run code". Then change the numbers and run again!
2 + 3
sqrt(144)
mean(c(4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42))
```
:::


## 5. Installing R and an IDE

You need to install **two** things, in this order:

1. **R** itself — the engine that actually runs the code.
2. **An IDE** (*Integrated Development Environment*) — the dashboard you use to write code, see results, plots and help. It is optional in principle, but in practice nobody works without one.

A useful analogy: R is the car engine; the IDE is the dashboard, steering wheel and seats.

### Step 1 — install R

Go to the CRAN website, <https://cran.r-project.org>, and choose your operating system:

- **Windows**: "Download R for Windows" → "base" → download the installer and run it, accepting the defaults.
- **macOS**: "Download R for macOS" → pick the installer that matches your processor (Apple silicon, i.e. M-series chips, or Intel). Open the `.pkg` file and follow the prompts.
- **Linux**: follow the instructions for your distribution (Ubuntu, Debian, Fedora, …) on the same page.

This course assumes **R 4.5 or newer** (the `penguins` dataset we use throughout was added to base R in version 4.5.0).

### Step 2 — install an IDE

Choose **one** of the two free IDEs developed by Posit:

| IDE | Download | Who it is for |
|---|---|---|
| **RStudio Desktop** | <https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/> | The classic, widely used IDE for R. Most tutorials and screenshots you find online use it. **Recommended for beginners.** |
| **Positron** | <https://positron.posit.co> | Posit's newer IDE, built on the same open-source foundation as Visual Studio Code. It supports R and Python side by side. |

Everything in this course works in both. When we describe menus we use RStudio's names; Positron has equivalent commands.

::: {.callout-note}
## Check your installation

Open your IDE and type `R.version.string` in the Console, then press Enter. You should see the version of R you just installed. If you see an older version, you probably have two R installations: uninstall the old one.
:::

## 6. A tour of RStudio

When you open RStudio you see **four panes**. Their position can be changed (*Tools → Global Options → Pane Layout*), but by default they are:

| Pane | Position | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| **Source (editor)** | top-left | Where you write and save **scripts** (`.R`) and **Quarto documents** (`.qmd`). Opens with *File → New File*. |
| **Console** | bottom-left | Where R actually runs. You can type commands here directly; results appear immediately. The `>` symbol is the *prompt*: R is waiting for you. |
| **Environment / History** | top-right | *Environment* lists the objects you have created (data, results). *History* lists the commands you have run. |
| **Files / Plots / Packages / Help / Viewer** | bottom-right | Browse files, see plots, manage installed packages, read help pages. |

The most useful keyboard shortcut to learn on day one: **Ctrl + Enter** (Windows/Linux) or **Cmd + Enter** (macOS) sends the current line of your script to the Console and runs it.

::: {.callout-tip}
## A setting worth changing right now

In *Tools → Global Options → General*, **untick** "Restore .RData into workspace at startup" and set "Save workspace to .RData on exit" to **Never**. This forces you to keep everything important in scripts, which is the heart of reproducible work. We explain why in [First steps](02-first-steps.qmd).
:::

## 7. Packages: installing and loading

Base R already contains thousands of functions, but sooner or later you will need a package. Using a package is a **two-step** process:

| Step | Function | How often? | Analogy |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Install** — download it from CRAN to your computer | `install.packages("name")` | **once** per computer (and after updating R) | buying a book and putting it on your shelf |
| **Load** — make its functions available in the current session | `library(name)` | **every** time you start R | taking the book off the shelf to read it |


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
install.packages("ggplot2")   # quotes are required here
library(ggplot2)              # quotes are not needed here
```
:::


This chunk is not run on the website (installing packages from a web page makes no sense), but you should run it on your own computer.

You can also install several packages at once:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
install.packages(c("dplyr", "tidyr", "readr"))
```
:::


To use a single function from a package *without* loading the whole package, write `package::function()`. For example, `dplyr::glimpse(penguins)`. We use this style in the course when a package is needed only once.

### The course installer

To save you time, the course provides a script that installs every package used in the lessons. Run this line once, in the Console:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
source("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/gianluca-sottile/An-R-Tutorial-for-Beginners/master/scripts/install-packages.R")
```
:::


`source()` runs an R script; here the script is read directly from the course's GitHub repository. It may take a while the first time.

### Where am I? `sessionInfo()`

When you ask for help (on a forum, or to your teacher), always say which version of R and of the packages you are using. One function prints all of it:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
sessionInfo()
```

::: {.callout-tip .read-output}
## How to read this output

- The first line is your **R version** (here R version 4.6.1 (2026-06-24)).
- **Platform** and **Running under** describe your computer and operating system.
- **attached base packages** are loaded automatically every time R starts (`stats`, `graphics`, `utils`, `datasets`, …). The `datasets` package is the reason why `penguins`, `mtcars` and `iris` are always available.
- **other attached packages** (if any) are those you loaded with `library()`, with their version numbers.
:::

::: {.callout-warning .pitfall}
## Common pitfalls

1. **Installing only an IDE.** RStudio and Positron need R to be installed separately. Install R first.
2. **Forgetting the quotes in `install.packages()`.** `install.packages(dplyr)` fails because R looks for an *object* called `dplyr`. Use `install.packages("dplyr")`.
3. **Putting `install.packages()` inside a script.** Every time the script runs it downloads the package again. Install once from the Console; keep only `library()` in your scripts.
4. **"there is no package called …"** when calling `library()`. It means the package is not installed (or the name is misspelled — R is case-sensitive: `library(ggplot2)`, not `library(GGplot2)`).
5. **Saving the workspace (`.RData`) on exit.** Old objects silently reappear in your next session and hide mistakes. Change the setting described in Section 6.
:::

## 8. Check your understanding

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q1. What is the difference between R and RStudio?

R is the language and the engine that executes the code. RStudio (like Positron) is an IDE: a program that makes it comfortable to write R code, see results, plots and help. You can use R without RStudio, but not RStudio without R.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q2. You installed `dplyr` yesterday. Today you restart R and `filter()` does not behave as expected. What did you probably forget?

To **load** the package with `library(dplyr)`. Installation happens once; loading must be done in every new session.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q3. Why is a script better than clicking through menus?

Because a script is a precise, re-runnable record of every step. You (or anyone else) can re-run the whole analysis on new data, check it for errors and see exactly how each result was obtained. This is **reproducibility**.
:::

## 9. Exercises

### Interactive (run in your browser)

::: {.exercise}
[★]{.stars} **Exercise 1 — R as a calculator.** Use R to compute: (a) the number of seconds in a day; (b) the square root of 2; (c) the average of 12, 15 and 21. Replace each `______`.


::: {.cell layout-align="center" exercise='ex_01_1'}
```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_01_1
______ * 60 * 60     # (a) seconds in a day
sqrt(______)         # (b)
(12 + 15 + 21) / ______   # (c)
```
:::


::: {.hint exercise="ex_01_1"}
A day has 24 hours. For (c), divide the sum by how many numbers you added.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_01_1"}
```r
24 * 60 * 60
sqrt(2)
(12 + 15 + 21) / 3
```
A day has 86,400 seconds; $\sqrt 2 \approx 1.414$; the average is 16. You could also write `mean(c(12, 15, 21))`.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★]{.stars} **Exercise 2 — which R am I running?** Print the version of R that runs in your browser, and then the full session information.


::: {.cell layout-align="center" exercise='ex_01_2'}
```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_01_2
R.version.______
______()
```
:::


::: {.hint exercise="ex_01_2"}
The first is a variable called `R.version.string`. The second is the function described in Section 7.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_01_2"}
```r
R.version.string
sessionInfo()
```
The browser runs webR, an R build compiled for the web: the *Platform* line therefore mentions `emscripten`/`wasm` instead of Windows or macOS.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★★]{.stars} **Exercise 3 — your first look at data.** The `penguins` dataset is always available in R ≥ 4.5. Use `nrow()` to count the penguins, `head()` to see the first rows and `summary()` to get an overview of every column.


::: {.cell layout-align="center" exercise='ex_01_3'}
```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_01_3
nrow(______)
head(______)
summary(______)
```
:::


::: {.hint exercise="ex_01_3"}
All three functions take the dataset itself as their argument: `penguins`.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_01_3"}
```r
nrow(penguins)
head(penguins)
summary(penguins)
```
There are 344 penguins. In the `summary()` output, notice the `NA's` lines: some measurements are missing. You will learn how to deal with them in [Missing data](../04-io/20-missing-data.qmd).
:::
:::

### Practice on your own computer

::: {.exercise}
[★]{.stars} **Exercise 4 — set up your machine.** (a) Install R and RStudio Desktop (or Positron). (b) In the Console, run `R.version.string` and check that the version is 4.5 or newer. (c) Install the `ggplot2` package and load it. (d) Change the workspace settings described in Section 6.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```r
R.version.string            # e.g. "R version 4.6.0 (...)"
install.packages("ggplot2")
library(ggplot2)            # no output means success
```
If `library(ggplot2)` prints nothing, it worked: in R, silence usually means success. Messages in red are not always errors — read them: lines starting with `Error` are errors, others are often just information.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★★]{.stars} **Exercise 5 — the course packages.** Run the course installer from Section 7. When it finishes, run `library(dplyr)` and `library(ggplot2)` and then `sessionInfo()`. Find the two packages and their version numbers in the output.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```r
source("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/gianluca-sottile/An-R-Tutorial-for-Beginners/master/scripts/install-packages.R")
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
sessionInfo()
```
They appear under **other attached packages**, e.g. `ggplot2_4.x.x` and `dplyr_1.x.x`. If the installer reports that a package failed, try installing that one alone with `install.packages()` and read the error message carefully.
:::
:::

## Summary

| Idea / function | What it means |
|---|---|
| R | Free, open-source language for statistics, data analysis and graphics |
| RStudio Desktop, Positron | IDEs: the environment where you write and run R code |
| CRAN | Official repository of R packages |
| `install.packages("pkg")` | Download and install a package (once) |
| `library(pkg)` | Load an installed package (every session) |
| `pkg::fun()` | Use one function without loading the package |
| `sessionInfo()`, `R.version.string` | Which version of R and packages you are running |

- R is a language built for data: scripts make your analysis **reproducible**.
- Install **R first**, then an IDE (RStudio Desktop or Positron).
- Packages are installed **once** and loaded **every session**.
- R cooperates with other tools; the skills you learn here transfer.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
